stories.headline: Plastic leachates harm coral reefs; Maui Huliau video on plastics
stories.summary: UH Mānoa research finds chemicals from plastics disrupt coral reproduction, followed by a Maui Huliau video on how pandemic-era masks and takeout add to ocean plastic.
stories.text: Plastic pollution is a large problem throughout the world. Marine animals are especially impacted as a lot of plastic ends up in the ocean. Sea Birds and fish ingest small bits of plastic called microplastic. Turtles swallow plastic bags believing them to be jellyfish. It also impacts humans when we consume fish that have ingested plastic. Animals like dolphins, sea turtles, sharks can become entangled in marine debris. Plastic production also contributes to climate change and air pollution. Unfortunately, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been an increase in plastic pollution. Face masks, plastic gloves, and other types of PPE are entering our ocean at a very alarming rate. Many of these single-use face masks are made out of the type of plastic that breaks up into smaller pieces. An estimated 1.56 billion face masks have entered our ocean in 2020. That's equivalent to nearly seven times all in the Earth. In addition, many more people are ordering takeout than before, which is leading to more plastic takeout containers and some used cutlery being thrown away and potentially ending up in the ocean. Luckily, there are some solutions to stop the COVID pandemic from becoming a plastic pandemic. One thing you can do is to use reusable cloth masks to stop disposable face masks from going into the ocean. Another solution is to bring your own container when ordering takeout. Visit restaurants that have composable containers or bring your own utensils from home. Even after the COVID pandemic, we can help stop single-use plastics by switching Switching to reusable bottles and switching to wooden are reusable utensils when eating food. By doing this, you can help protect our oceans from the impact of plastic pollution. Join us in a fight against plastic pollution. Boy, we need to all be a part of that solution.

The younger generation, they see that, they want to eat healthy, they want to be like Cap. He's 55 years old and he's still climbing the tree. It's not a movement, but it's more so an educational beast of what we need to do for our young generation. Because when I went out there, it was really sad, like I said, to see some of the directors for the Department of Ag, The DOE, the governor's office, hugged me when I first got there. And then the next time I came back up, they were in wheelchairs. Next time I came, they were like had half of their foot cut off. You know, it scared me to do what I did 13 years ago, you know, lose weight. But more importantly, it's the food that we eat. And the food that we eat is here, right here in the islands. You know, we grow it, we look at it, we see it, we let it fall on the ground and get rotten. I mean, I'm like, wait a minute, man, we gotta, we gotta change this. I think the things that CAP does is just remarkable. You know, to do things like 100 years ago that they used to do it, it's really a team effort of people working together to bring this opportunity to share our food to the world. We got an important message to let people know that our health really can get better if we eat the right stuff. I've added to my food list, of course, breadfruit, sweet potatoes, kalo, luau li. We gotta get some of our weak leaders in the right direction. I mean weak leaders. They want to keep us unhealthy. Because they can control us. Remember that. Don't drink the kule. Hey, come on you guys. Just come and sit. Don't drink the kule. Yeah. Drink the coconut water. Love ʻUlu.

stories.headline: Hawaiʻi band chosen for 2026 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
stories.summary: Nā Koa Aliʻi Aloha Ball-State Marching Band, one of 10 bands selected, will perform in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
stories.text: The countdown to the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has begun, celebrating a century of holiday tradition. Hawaiʻi's own Nākoa ʻAlii ʻAloha Ball-State Marching Band was Aloha is chosen from a national pool to perform in the 2026 Parade. One of just 10 bands selected, this marks the group's fourth appearance in the iconic New York City events.

stories.headline: Festivals of Aloha returns to Four Seasons Wailea in October
stories.summary: The 4th Annual Festivals of Aloha at the Four Seasons Resort in Wailea features Hawaiian practitioners, live performances and educational experiences.
stories.text: The 4th Annual Festivals of Aloha is happening at the Four Seasons Resort in Wailea from Friday, October 24th through Sunday, October 26th, featuring a weekend of events showcasing authentic Hawaiian practitioners, offering live performances and educational experiences.

stories.summary: The fair returned after a six-year absence, drawing 30,000 on opening night and more than 115,000 over four days, with the mayor interviewed by host Joe Abella.

stories.headline: Maui rain gauges show well below normal levels
stories.summary: Most Maui rain gauges show subpar levels, and Pu'u Kukui's single-day high of 2.18 inches on September 11 was only 28% of its long-term average.
stories.text: Rain. There isn't any. And we desperately need some. Soon. Most rain gauges on Maui are showing subpar levels. And although one of the wettest places on earth, Puʻu Kukui logged a single day The highest level of 2.18 inches, September 11th, it represents only 28 percent of its long-term average.

stories.headline: Land board orders two appraisals for West Maui windmill lease
stories.summary: After an executive session, the Board of Land & Natural Resources ordered an appraisal both ways, bare land and land plus improvements, with an eight-week deadline on the Kaheawa Wind Power lease.
stories.text: No rain, but we do have wind. The Board of Land and Natural Resources met on September 26th regarding the West Maui windmills, direct lease to Kaheʻava wind power. The main dispute The board's first meeting was on how to evaluate the appraisal, bare land versus land plus improvements, and disagreements over turbine upgrades. After an executive session, the board made an amendment to order an appraisal both ways with an eight-week deadline.

stories.headline: State to open 64-unit Kipuola kauhale tiny home village
stories.summary: The state will move homeless people into a 64-unit tiny home village near the airport as an alternative to a tent city on DOT land where 16 people have died.
stories.text: A tiny house is far better than no house, I suppose. The state of Hawaiʻi is about to welcome homeless people into a 64-unit Kīpuhuola Kauhale Tiny Home Village near the intersection of Elmer-Krewaljoway and Hana Highway. That's just outside the airport. The prefab dwellings are made in Korea and cost $20,542 each. The The project is an alternative to a crime-ridden tent city on DOT land near Servco that housed 129 houseless people and where 16 people have died. The 13 tents still on site currently shelter 57 residents including three couples and their dogs and cats.

stories.headline: About 2,000 Kaiser employees plan five-day strike October 14
stories.summary: Kaiser says it offered a 20% raise over four years and operations will continue during the strike, though some non-urgent appointments may be rescheduled.
stories.text: At press time, about 2,000 Kaiser Permanente employees are planning a five-day strike beginning October 14th. Kaiser says they have offered a 20% raise over four years and that operations will continue during the strike, although some non-urgent appointments may be rescheduled.

stories.headline: Hawaii concealed carry law headed to U.S. Supreme Court
stories.summary: The Hawaii Rifle Association wants the Supreme Court to remove the state's default ban on concealed handguns in private spaces unless signs allow guns.
stories.text: There is a shootout, metaphorically speaking, coming to the United States Supreme Court over strict gun rights in Hawaiʻi that limit where someone can carry a concealed weapon. Hawaiʻi law bans concealed handguns in private spaces like beaches, parks, and businesses unless guns-allowed signs are posted. The Hawaiʻi Rifle Association wants to change The law to remove the gun-free zone by default provision that they say encourages criminals to come and take your stuff.

stories.headline: Governor Green travels to Japan for Okinawan immigration anniversary
stories.summary: Governor Green left Saturday for Okinowa to mark the 125th anniversary of Okinowan immigration to Hawaii.
stories.text: Governor Green is on the road again. This time, our well-traveled chief executive is off to Japan. He took off Saturday to Okinawa to celebrate the 125th anniversary of Okinawan

stories.headline: MEO offers up to $25,000 grants to wildfire survivors
stories.summary: Maui Economic Opportunity, backed by the Maui Strong Fund, is giving disaster stabilization grants of up to $25,000 for housing, utilities, transportation, restoration and health care.
stories.text: Maui Economic Opportunity, or MEO, with support from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation's Maui Strong Fund, is providing up to $25,000 in disaster stabilization grants to wildfire survivors for housing, utilities, transportation, restoration, and health care needs. Since Of the 2023 wildfires, MEO has assisted over a thousand families with housing, 6,400 individuals through the Maui Relief Fund program, and has helped many, many Maui families in other ways.

stories.headline: Hawaii to host world's largest land-based seaweed farm
stories.summary: The Kona seaweed farm will expand from a half acre to 15 acres, and its limu kohu supplement aims to cut cattle methane emissions by up to 83%.
stories.text: Hawaiʻi will become home to the world's largest land-based seaweed farm, expanding Expanding from a half-acre to 15 acres at Kona Big Island's Aquaculture Park. Their Limu Kōhu supplement aims to reduce cow flatulence and cut cattle methane emissions by up to 83 percent, and the expansion is expected to bring new jobs and global market reach.

stories.headline: Aloha Classic windsurfing returns to Ho'okipa October 13 to 24
stories.summary: The annual windsurfing event draws top riders from more than 40 countries, followed by a clip from a previous Aloha Classic.
stories.text: Once you're an Aloha Classic Champion, you're always an Aloha Classic Champion. But nobody ever said it was easy getting there. Sometimes, the ocean reminds you who's boss. Boards break, Rigs snap, and yeah, you might leave a little skin on the reef. But then, there's the magic. When everything lines up, and for a few seconds you're not fighting the ocean, you're dancing with it. This is the arena of windsurfing. The legends, the rookies, the women, the youth, the masters, all thrown down in the same lineup. From the first generation that built this sport to the new crew carrying it forward, this event is where the story keeps getting written. So yeah, an Aloha Classic Champion. But first, you gotta earn it. How do you feel? I feel really good.

stories.headline: UH enrollment reaches 51,411, highest since 2017
stories.summary: University of Hawaii enrollment rose 5.1% since 2023, and UH Maui College climbed 7.3% to 2,997 students.
stories.text: Enrollment across the ten campuses of the University of Hawaiʻi rose to 51,411 students this fall. The highest enrollment since 2017. It marks the third straight year of growth and a 5.1% rise since 2023. UH Maui College saw enrollment climb 7.3% to 2,997 students. Growth was fueled by more first-time freshmen and high school dual credit programs.

stories.headline: Digital Navigator program offers free tech help at libraries
stories.summary: The program launches today at five Oahu libraries and will expand statewide to help patrons with email, devices, job applications and online safety.
stories.text: Residents on Maui will soon have access to free one-on-one tech help through the new digital navigator program announced by Lieutenant Governor Sylvia Luke and the Hawaiʻi State Public Library System. The initiative launches today, October 6th, at five Oʻahu libraries and will expand statewide in the upcoming weeks. Trained navigators will assist patrons with email setup, device use, online services, job applications, and cybersecurity awareness. The statewide partnership is an attempt to close Hawaiʻi's digital divide and build community confidence in the use of technology.

stories.headline: MACC hosts Maui showcase of Hawaii International Film Festival
stories.summary: The showcase runs November 8 to 9 at the McCoy Studio Theater with nine documentaries and one drama short, followed by a clip from Lahaina Rising.
stories.text: I'll never forget how dark it was. A cloud of smoke so massive that it was blocking out the sun. I get a call. There's a fire. We realized Lahaina was in serious trouble.
